title: Writing the General Solution
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: When no interval is specified, a trigonometric equation usually requires a general solution: a mathematical expression that represents every angle satisfying the equation. Because trigonometric functions are periodic, a single equation can have infinitely many solutions. The general solution captures this repeating pattern using an integer parameter such as n ∈ ℤ. Writing a correct general solution requires understanding the function's period, all solution branches within one period, the effect of multiple angles such as 2x or 3x, and any domain restrictions.

content.text: A general solution is an expression that represents every value of the variable satisfying a trigonometric equation.
For example, tan(x) = 1 has infinitely many solutions because tangent repeats every π radians. Instead of listing π/4, 5π/4, 9π/4, and so on, we write x = π/4 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
The integer n generates all repeated solutions. Positive, negative, and zero integer values of n allow the formula to represent solutions in both directions along the number line.
The symbol n is usually used to represent any integer, allowing the formula to generate infinitely many solutions.
The symbol n usually represents any integer, meaning n ∈ ℤ. Substituting different integer values produces the complete infinite sequence of solutions.
For x = θ + 2nπ, n = 0 gives θ, n = 1 gives θ + 2π, n = −1 gives θ − 2π, and so on.
Never restrict n to positive integers unless the problem specifically says so.

sections.title: The Period Determines the General Solution

content.text: The general solution depends on the period of the trigonometric function involved.
The period is the amount by which the angle can be increased while leaving the function value unchanged.
Sine and cosine have period 2π, while tangent and cotangent have period π.
Therefore, sine and cosine general solutions normally repeat using 2nπ, whereas tangent and cotangent solutions normally repeat using nπ.
Reciprocal functions inherit the periods of their corresponding functions: secant has period 2π, cosecant has period 2π, and cotangent has period π.
For sin(x) = a, first determine a principal angle θ = sin⁻¹(a). Sine has the same value at θ and π − θ within one 2π cycle.
Therefore, the two solution branches can be written as x = θ + 2nπ and x = π − θ + 2nπ.
An equivalent compact form is x = (−1)ⁿ sin⁻¹(a) + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
The two-branch form is often easier to understand and use when solving problems manually, while the compact form is useful for expressing all solutions in a single formula.
For cos(x) = a, let θ = cos⁻¹(a). Cosine has the same value at θ and −θ, or equivalently at θ and 2π − θ within one cycle.
The general solution is x = ±θ + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
An equivalent two-branch form is x = θ + 2nπ or x = 2π − θ + 2nπ.
For tan(x) = a, let θ = tan⁻¹(a). Tangent repeats every π radians, so every solution differs from θ by an integer multiple of π.
The general solution is x = θ + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.
Unlike sine and cosine, tangent does not require two separate branches when its equation is written as tan(x) = a.
Secant, cosecant, and cotangent equations are usually rewritten using reciprocal identities before solving.
For sec(x) = a, rewrite it as cos(x) = 1/a, provided a ≠ 0 and the resulting cosine value lies in [−1, 1].
For csc(x) = a, rewrite it as sin(x) = 1/a, provided a ≠ 0 and the resulting sine value lies in [−1, 1].
For cot(x) = a, rewrite it as tan(x) = 1/a, provided a ≠ 0.
Domain restrictions must still be checked because reciprocal functions are undefined wherever their denominator is zero.
Some equations have especially simple general solutions. For example, sin(x) = 0 occurs at every integer multiple of π, while cos(x) = 0 occurs at every odd multiple of π/2.
Tangent equals zero whenever sine is zero and cosine is nonzero, giving x = nπ.
Secant and cosecant can never equal zero because they are reciprocals of cosine and sine.
For equations such as sin(2x) = a, first solve for the complete set of values of 2x.
For example, if sin(2x) = a and the general solutions for y are y = α + 2nπ or y = π − α + 2nπ, substitute y = 2x and divide every complete solution by 2.
Thus x = α/2 + nπ or x = (π − α)/2 + nπ.
The same principle applies to cos(kx), tan(kx), and equations containing more complicated angle expressions.
For an equation such as sin(3x − π/4) = a, treat the entire angle 3x − π/4 as the unknown angle first.
Solve the trigonometric equation for the composite angle, generate every required branch, and only then solve the resulting algebraic equations for x.
Failing to generate every branch before isolating x can cause valid solutions to be missed.

sections.title: Using Identities Before Writing the General Solution

content.text: Many equations cannot immediately be written in a standard form. They may first require identities, factoring, substitution, or algebraic manipulation.
For example, an equation such as 2sin²(x) − 1 = 0 can be transformed into sin²(x) = 1/2 and then into sin(x) = ±1/√2.
Both signs must be considered before constructing the general solution.
The final answer should represent every solution of the original equation, not merely every solution of an intermediate equation.

sections.title: General Solutions in Degrees and Radians

content.text: General solutions can be written in degrees or radians, but the units must remain consistent throughout the solution.
Sine and cosine repeat every 360° or 2π radians, while tangent and cotangent repeat every 180° or π radians.
Do not combine degree measures with radian measures in the same formula.
A restricted solution lists only the solutions lying inside a specified interval such as 0 ≤ x < 2π or 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
A general solution represents all solutions, usually through an integer parameter n.
If a question asks for the general solution, do not stop after listing the solutions in one revolution.
If a question specifies an interval, use the general solution as a pattern and then select only the values that lie inside the requested interval.
A general solution should be checked conceptually and, when necessary, algebraically.
Check that the formula reproduces known solutions for several integer values of n and that increasing n moves between solutions by the correct period.
If algebraic transformations such as squaring, multiplying by an expression that might be zero, or taking reciprocals were used, substitute the final solutions back into the original equation.
Domain restrictions must also be respected.
The infinite nature of the solution set comes from periodicity. Once one solution is known, adding an integer multiple of the function's period produces another solution.
For sine and cosine, the fundamental period is 2π. For tangent and cotangent, it is π.
When the input is multiplied by k, such as sin(kx), the resulting function has period 2π/|k|. This is why multiple-angle equations can have more solutions within a fixed interval.

sections.title: Systematic Method for Writing General Solutions

content.text: First simplify the equation until it is in a solvable trigonometric form.
Next identify the trigonometric function and determine its period.
Find every solution branch for one complete period.
Introduce the appropriate integer parameter n.
If the equation contains kx or another composite angle, solve for the complete angle expression first and then isolate x.
Finally check domain restrictions and substitute into the original equation when transformations could have introduced or removed solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine General Solution
formulas.expression: sin(x) = a  ⇒  x = (−1)ⁿ sin⁻¹(a) + nπ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Compact formula representing every real solution of sin(x) = a.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Two-Branch General Solution
formulas.expression: sin(x) = sin(θ)  ⇒  x = θ + 2nπ  OR  x = π − θ + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: The two branches arise because sine has the same value at θ and π − θ in one 2π cycle.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine General Solution
formulas.explanation: Represents every real solution of a cosine equation.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Two-Branch General Solution
formulas.expression: cos(x) = cos(θ)  ⇒  x = 2nπ ± θ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Equivalent form that directly uses cosine's symmetry.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent General Solution
formulas.expression: tan(x) = a  ⇒  x = tan⁻¹(a) + nπ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Uses tangent's π-periodicity.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Equal Tangent General Solution
formulas.expression: tan(x) = tan(θ)  ⇒  x = θ + nπ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Any two tangent angles with the same value differ by an integer multiple of π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Equals Zero
formulas.explanation: Sine is zero at every integer multiple of π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Equals Zero
formulas.expression: cos(x) = 0  ⇒  x = π/2 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Cosine is zero at every odd multiple of π/2.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Equals Zero
formulas.explanation: Tangent is zero whenever sine is zero and cosine is nonzero.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Secant General Solution
formulas.expression: sec(x) = a  ⇒  cos(x) = 1/a  ⇒  x = ±cos⁻¹(1/a) + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Valid for a ≠ 0 and |a| ≥ 1. Domain restrictions must also be satisfied.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosecant General Solution
formulas.expression: csc(x) = a  ⇒  sin(x) = 1/a  ⇒  x = (−1)ⁿ sin⁻¹(1/a) + nπ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Valid for a ≠ 0 and |a| ≥ 1, with the original cosecant domain respected.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cotangent General Solution
formulas.expression: cot(x) = a  ⇒  tan(x) = 1/a  ⇒  x = tan⁻¹(1/a) + nπ, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Valid for a ≠ 0. Cotangent has period π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Secant Domain
formulas.expression: sec(x) is defined only when cos(x) ≠ 0
formulas.explanation: Secant is undefined at x = π/2 + nπ.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosecant Domain
formulas.expression: csc(x) is defined only when sin(x) ≠ 0
formulas.explanation: Cosecant is undefined at x = nπ.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cotangent Domain
formulas.expression: cot(x) is defined only when sin(x) ≠ 0
formulas.explanation: Cotangent is undefined wherever sine is zero.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Secant Cannot Equal Zero
formulas.explanation: Secant is the reciprocal of cosine, so it can never equal zero.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosecant Cannot Equal Zero
formulas.explanation: Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine, so it can never equal zero.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Period
formulas.explanation: Sine repeats every 2π radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Period
formulas.explanation: Cosine repeats every 2π radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Period
formulas.explanation: Tangent repeats every π radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cotangent Period
formulas.explanation: Cotangent repeats every π radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Secant Period
formulas.explanation: Secant has the same fundamental period as cosine.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosecant Period
formulas.explanation: Cosecant has the same fundamental period as sine.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of sin(kx)
formulas.explanation: Multiplying the input by k compresses the graph horizontally and reduces the period.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of cos(kx)
formulas.explanation: Useful for understanding the number of repetitions and solutions in an interval.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of tan(kx)
formulas.explanation: The tangent period becomes smaller when the input is multiplied by k.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Solving sin(kx) = a
formulas.expression: sin(kx) = a  ⇒  kx = (−1)ⁿ sin⁻¹(a) + nπ  ⇒  x = [(−1)ⁿ sin⁻¹(a) + nπ]/k, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Solve the complete equation for the multiple angle kx before dividing by k.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Solving cos(kx) = a
formulas.expression: cos(kx) = a  ⇒  kx = ±cos⁻¹(a) + 2nπ  ⇒  x = [±cos⁻¹(a) + 2nπ]/k, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Generate both cosine branches before isolating x.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Solving tan(kx) = a
formulas.expression: tan(kx) = a  ⇒  kx = tan⁻¹(a) + nπ  ⇒  x = [tan⁻¹(a) + nπ]/k, n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Tangent contributes its π-periodicity before the division by k.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Degree-Radian Conversion
formulas.explanation: The fundamental conversion relationship between degrees and radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Degrees to Radians
formulas.explanation: Multiply a degree measure by π/180 to convert it to radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Radians to Degrees
formulas.explanation: Multiply a radian measure by 180/π to convert it to degrees.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine and Cosine Period in Degrees
formulas.explanation: Sine and cosine repeat every 360 degrees.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Period in Degrees
formulas.explanation: Tangent and cotangent repeat every 180 degrees.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Range
formulas.explanation: Therefore sin(x) = a has real solutions only when −1 ≤ a ≤ 1.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Range
formulas.explanation: Therefore cos(x) = a has real solutions only when −1 ≤ a ≤ 1.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Range
formulas.explanation: Tangent can take every real value, although it is undefined at x = π/2 + nπ.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Reciprocal Identities
formulas.explanation: Useful for converting reciprocal-function equations into sine, cosine, or tangent equations.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] General Periodic Solution Rule
formulas.expression: If f(x) = f(x + T), then x = θ + nT, n ∈ ℤ, whenever θ is a solution and T is the relevant period
formulas.explanation: This is the underlying principle behind general solutions of periodic equations.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Verify Solutions in the Original Equation
formulas.expression: Candidate solution  →  substitute into the original equation  →  accept only if the original equation is satisfied
formulas.explanation: Essential when transformations may introduce extraneous solutions or violate domain restrictions.

examples.question: Find the general solution of sin(x) = 1/2.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/6 because sin(π/6) = 1/2. Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II. Therefore x = π/6 + 2nπ or x = 5π/6 + 2nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of cos(x) = −1/2.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/3. Cosine is negative in Quadrants II and III. Therefore x = 2π/3 + 2nπ or x = 4π/3 + 2nπ, where n ∈ ℤ. Equivalently, x = ±2π/3 + 2nπ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of tan(x) = √3.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/3 because tan(π/3) = √3. Tangent has period π, so x = π/3 + nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of sin(x) = 0.
examples.solution: Sine is zero at 0, π, 2π, and every integer multiple of π. Therefore x = nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of cos(x) = 0.
examples.solution: Cosine is zero at π/2 and 3π/2 in one revolution. Since the solutions are separated by π, the general solution is x = π/2 + nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of sec(x) = 2.
examples.solution: Rewrite the equation as cos(x) = 1/2. Therefore x = ±π/3 + 2nπ, where n ∈ ℤ. Equivalently, x = π/3 + 2nπ or x = 5π/3 + 2nπ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of csc(x) = −2.
examples.solution: Rewrite as sin(x) = −1/2. The solutions are x = 7π/6 + 2nπ or x = 11π/6 + 2nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of cot(x) = 1.
examples.solution: Since cot(x) = 1 means tan(x) = 1, the reference angle is π/4. Tangent has period π, so x = π/4 + nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of sin(2x) = 1/2.
examples.solution: Let y = 2x. Then sin(y) = 1/2, so y = π/6 + 2nπ or y = 5π/6 + 2nπ. Since y = 2x, divide by 2: x = π/12 + nπ or x = 5π/12 + nπ, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of cos(3x) = 0.
examples.solution: For cos(y) = 0, y = π/2 + nπ. Let y = 3x. Then 3x = π/2 + nπ, so x = π/6 + nπ/3, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of tan(2x) = 1.
examples.solution: For tan(y) = 1, y = π/4 + nπ. Set y = 2x. Then 2x = π/4 + nπ, giving x = π/8 + nπ/2, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of sin(2x − π/3) = 0.
examples.solution: Let y = 2x − π/3. Since sin(y) = 0, y = nπ. Therefore 2x − π/3 = nπ. Solving for x gives x = π/6 + nπ/2, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of 2sin²(x) − 1 = 0.
examples.solution: Rearrange: 2sin²(x) = 1, so sin²(x) = 1/2. Therefore sin(x) = ±1/√2. The corresponding angles are x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, and 7π/4 in one 2π cycle. A compact general solution is x = π/4 + nπ/2, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Find the general solution of sin(x) = √3/2 in degrees.
examples.solution: The reference angle is 60°. Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II, so x = 60° + 360°n or x = 120° + 360°n, where n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Explain why tan(x) = 2 has infinitely many solutions.
examples.solution: Tangent has period π. If θ = tan⁻¹(2) is one solution, then θ + nπ is also a solution for every integer n. Therefore the general solution is x = tan⁻¹(2) + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: For x = π/4 + nπ, what happens when n = −1?
examples.solution: Substituting n = −1 gives x = π/4 − π = −3π/4. This is a valid solution because the general solution includes negative angles as well as positive angles.

examples.question: Find the general solution of 2sin(x) = 3.
examples.solution: Rearrange to sin(x) = 3/2. Since the range of sine is [−1, 1], sine cannot equal 3/2. Therefore there is no real solution.

examples.question: Find the general solution of sec(x) = 1/2.
examples.solution: Rewrite as cos(x) = 2. Since cosine can only take values from −1 to 1, cos(x) = 2 is impossible. Therefore there is no real solution.

key_ideas: A general solution represents every solution, not just the solutions in one revolution.
n represents any integer, so always state n ∈ ℤ.
The period determines how solutions repeat.
Sine and cosine normally use 2nπ in their general solutions.
Tangent and cotangent normally use nπ because their period is π.
Sine equations generally have two solution branches in one 2π cycle.
Cosine equations can be expressed using ±θ or two explicit branches.
Tangent equations require only one branch plus integer multiples of π.
Secant, cosecant, and cotangent equations can usually be converted to cosine, sine, and tangent equations.
Reciprocal-function domain restrictions must be checked.
Secant and cosecant can never equal zero.
For multiple-angle equations, solve for the complete multiple angle before isolating x.
Multiplying the angle by k changes the period and can increase the number of solutions in a fixed interval.
For composite angles such as ax + b, solve for the complete angle expression first.
When identities or algebraic transformations are used, the final solution must still satisfy the original equation.
General solutions may be written in degrees or radians, but the units must remain consistent.
Restricted solutions and general solutions are different types of answers.
The integer parameter allows the solution pattern to extend infinitely in both directions.
A correct general solution must contain every valid branch and must not include invalid values.
misconceptions: Forgetting to include n ∈ ℤ.
Giving only the solutions from 0 to 2π when a general solution is required.
Using 2π as the period for tangent.
Using π as the period for sine or cosine.
Finding only one solution branch for sine or cosine.
Dividing by the multiple-angle coefficient before generating all solutions.
Forgetting that a composite angle such as 3x − π/4 must be treated as the complete angle first.
Mixing degrees and radians in the same solution.
Assuming every reciprocal-function equation has a solution.
Forgetting that sec(x) and csc(x) cannot equal zero.
Ignoring the domain of secant, cosecant, or cotangent.
Assuming that n must be positive.
Assuming negative values of n are invalid.
Writing a formula that generates only some of the solutions.
Accepting solutions introduced by an algebraic transformation without checking the original equation.
Using an inverse-trigonometric calculator result as the complete answer.
Forgetting that inverse trigonometric functions return principal values, not all possible solutions.
Assuming that the same general-solution formula works unchanged for every trigonometric function.
Forgetting that the period of sin(kx), cos(kx), and tan(kx) changes when the angle is multiplied by k.
Failing to check whether the equation has any real solution based on the range of the function.
